sense: a way out of a difficulty

terms.gloss: a remedy, a solution (to a problem)
evidence: Ter. Ph. 616: invēnī, opīnor, remedium huic reī
Ter. And. 468: quod remedium nunc huic malō inveniam?
terms.comment: Terence’s word whenever a slave or a son needs a way out, with the dative of the trouble (huic reī, huic malō). Also a medicine or cure (see remedy).

evidence: Cic. Att. 10.14.1: nūllīus cōnsilī exitum invēnimus
terms.comment: To find a way of doing something: ratiōnem invenīre (see approach, a way of dealing with something).
Classically the solving of a puzzle or an argument (see solution, the answer to a puzzle); Traupman uses it of a practical problem.

phrases.latin: Invēnī, opīnor, remedium huic reī. — Quid, Geta? — Quod remedium?
phrases.english: I think I’ve found a way out of this. — What is it, Geta? — What way out?

phrases.latin: Quod remedium nunc huic malō inveniam?
phrases.english: What way out can I find from this trouble now?

phrases.latin: numquam exitum inveniēs. Nēmō cum sarcinīs ēnatat.
phrases.english: You will never find a way out. Nobody swims to safety with his luggage.
For any pain, the remedy is patience.

sources: Lewis & Short: remedium · Lewis & Short: exitus · Lewis & Short: solutio
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 185, 382.
